intro: Variation VII, “Troyte” (Presto), from Elgar’s Variations on an Original Theme “Enigma”, Op. 36, is an orchestral joke about the architect Arthur Troyte Griffith’s struggles at the piano. The timpani and low strings depict his clumsy playing.

sections.label: Var 7 · “Troyte”, Presto, at the piano
sections.mNote: Timpani and low strings hammer out the joke.

cues.title: Opening, timpani and low strings
cues.text: Timpani, cellos and double basses play a lopsided figure. Elgar writes one semibreve beat to each bar and marks the music Presto. The winds enter while the bass repeats its few notes.
cues.evidence: Novello full score, p. 35, rehearsal 23: 1/1 metre, opening timpani and low strings, followed by wind entries. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/1e/IMSLP23792-PMLP07276-Elgar_-_Enigma_Variations_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Troyte Griffith and the piano lesson
cues.text: Troyte Griffith was a Malvern architect and one of Elgar’s closest friends. In Elgar’s account the variation depicts a piano lesson that gets steadily worse. The pupil blunders, the teacher tries to restore order and ends the lesson with a final slam. Elgar identified the teacher as himself.
cues.evidence: Elgar, My Friends Pictured Within (Novello), section VII, identifies himself as the instructor and explains the final slam. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/0/06/IMSLP339677-SIBLEY1802.27173.6d2a-39087004945996text.pdf. The lifelong friendship is documented at https://elgar.org/3enigma.htm

source.title: Elgar, Enigma Variations, full score (Novello)
source.locator: Novello full score, pp. 35–46, rehearsal figures 23–29: Variation VII, Troyte, marked Presto.

timeline.note: Timpani, cellos and double basses begin the lopsided figure that drives Troyte’s piano lesson (p. 35).
Woodwinds rise in short phrases; strings and brass answer with accented chords. The timpani play repeated strokes beneath them (pp. 35–36).
Both violin sections run up and down against sharp accents in the wind and brass. A rising scale in the woodwind leads back to the timpani figure (pp. 38–39).
The violins play twelve-note runs, marked brillante. Bassoons, violas and cellos take up the runs while the timpani repeat their figure (pp. 40–42).
The violin runs return over the bass. Horns and trumpets climb with the woodwinds; trombones and tuba rejoin at rehearsal 28 (pp. 42–44).
The second flute changes to piccolo for the rising wind scale. The strings rise beneath it, and the brass plays another heavy reply (pp. 44–45).
The brass holds a chord while the strings descend in triplets. Timpani and cymbals join the final stroke (p. 46).

composer.epithet: Composer of the Enigma Variations, a set of variations drawn from his friendships, who also recorded his own music for the gramophone.
facts: His father’s Worcester music shop; violin and organ; composition largely self-taught
Powick bandmaster, instrumental teacher and organist at St George’s, Worcester
Two symphonies; violin and cello concertos; Gerontius; five Pomp and Circumstance marches
Master of the King’s Musick from 1924; recordings of his own orchestral works
composer.background:
Elgar grew up among the instruments and sheet music in his father’s Worcester shop. William tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church; Edward studied the scores, learned several instruments and earned money with his violin. Born at Lower Broadheath on 2 June 1857, he had hoped to study at Leipzig, but the family could not afford it. Playing in the Three Choirs Festival orchestra, he learned the choral music of Handel and Mendelssohn as a member of the string section.

From 1879 to 1884 he was bandmaster at Worcester County Asylum, Powick. He trained members of staff to play for the patients and supplied quadrilles and polkas for the Friday-evening dances. He knew each player in this orchestra individually and had to write within their capabilities. He also taught in local schools and gave private lessons in Malvern. In 1885 he succeeded William at the organ of St George’s.
